entries.6a67924cd18d0c489c7f8a2cfc7541ac3fc90892: <div sID="gen20400" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Mic.2" sID="Mic.2"/> <div eID="gen20400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20401" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20402" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The sins with which the people of Israel are charged—covetousness and oppression, fraudulent and violent practices (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.1-Mic.2.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), dealing barbarously, even with women and children, and other harmless people, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.8-Mic.2.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. Opposition of God's prophets and silencing them (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.6-Mic.2.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>), and delighting in false prophets, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">ver. 11</reference>. II. The judgments with which they are threatened for those sins, that they should be humbled, and impoverished (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.3-Mic.2.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), and banished, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">ver. 10</reference>. III. Gracious promises of comfort, reserved for the good people among them, in the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12-Mic.2.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. And this is the sum and scope of most of the chapters of this and other prophecies.
entries.08e53ff7a4d22b7d6a238ebe8c6e9c8e0b2bcfe6: <div eID="gen20402" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20401" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen20403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand. <hi type="super">2</hi> And they covet fields, and take <hi type="italic">them</hi> by violence; and houses, and take <hi type="italic">them</hi> away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time <hi type="italic">is</hi> evil. <hi type="super">4</hi> In that day shall <hi type="italic">one</hi> take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed <hi type="italic">it</hi> from me! turning away he hath divided our fields. <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore thou shalt have none that shall cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20404" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The injustice of man contriving the evil of sin, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1-Mic.2.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. God was coming forth against this people to destroy them, and here he shows what was the ground of his controversy with them; it is that which is often mentioned as a sin that hastens the ruin of nations and families as much as any, the sin of oppression. Let us see the steps of it. 1. They eagerly desire that which is not their own—that is the <hi type="italic">root of bitterness,</hi> the root of all evil, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">v. 2</reference>. They <hi type="italic">covet fields and houses,</hi> as Ahab did Naboth's vineyard. "Oh that such a one's field and house were mine! It lies convenient for me, and I would manage it better than he does; it is fitter for me than for him." 2. They set their wits on work to invent ways of accomplishing their desire (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">v. 4</reference>); they devise iniquity with a great deal of cursed art and policy; they plot how to do it effectually, and yet so as not to expose themselves, or bring themselves into danger, or under reproach, by it. This is called <hi type="italic">working evil!</hi> they are working it in their heads, in their families, and are as intent upon it, and with as much pleasure, as if they were doing it, and are as confident of their success (so wisely do they think they have laid the scheme) as if it were assuredly done. Note, It is bad to do mischief upon a sudden thought, but much worse to devise it, to do it with design and deliberation; when the craft and subtlety of the old serpent appear with his poison and venom, it is wickedness in perfection. They devised it <hi type="italic">upon their beds,</hi> when they should have been asleep; care to compass a mischievous design held their eyes waking. <hi type="italic">Upon their beds,</hi> where they should have been remembering God, and meditating upon him, where they should have been <hi type="italic">communing with their own hearts</hi> and examining them, they were <hi type="italic">devising iniquity.</hi> It is of great consequence to improve and employ the hours of our retirement and solitude in a proper manner. 3. They employ their power in executing what they have designed and contrived; they practise the iniquity they have devised, <hi type="italic">because it is in the power of their hand;</hi> they find that they can compass it by the help of their wealth, and the authority and interest they have, and that none dare control them, or call them to an account for it; and this, they think, will justify them and bear them out in it. Note, It is the mistake of many to think that as they can do they may do; whereas no power is given for destruction, but all for edification. 4. They are industrious and very expeditious in accomplishing the iniquity they have devised; when they have settled the matter in their thoughts, in their beds, they lose no time, but as soon as the <hi type="italic">morning is light</hi> they practice it; they are up early in the prosecution of their designs, and what ill their hand finds to do they do it <hi type="italic">with all their might,</hi> which shames our slothfulness and dilatoriness in doing good, and should shame us out of them. In the service of God, and our generation, let it never be said that we left that to be done to-morrow which we could do to-day. 5. They stick at nothing to compass their designs; what they <hi type="italic">covet</hi> they <hi type="italic">take away,</hi> if they can, and, (1.) They care not what wrong they do, though it be ever so gross and open; they take away men's fields by violence, not only by fraud, and underhand practices and colour of law, but by force and with a high hand. (2.) They care not to whom they do wrong nor how far the iniquity extends which they devise: They <hi type="italic">oppress a man and his house;</hi> they rob and ruin those that have numerous families to maintain, and are not concerned though they send them and their wives and children a begging. They <hi type="italic">oppress a man and his heritage;</hi> they take away from men that which they have an unquestionable title to, having received it from their ancestors, and which they have but in trust, to transmit it to their posterity; but those oppressors care not how many they impoverish, so they may but enrich themselves. Note, If covetousness reigns in the heart, commonly all compassion is banished from it; and if any man <hi type="italic">love this world,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">love of the Father,</hi> so the love of his neighbour <hi type="italic">is not in him.</hi> <div eID="gen20404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20405" type="x-p"/> II. The justice of God contriving the evil of punishment for this sin (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord,</hi> the righteous God, that judges between man and man, and is an avenger on those that do wrong, <hi type="italic">Behold, against this family do I devise an evil,</hi> that is, against the whole kingdom, the <hi type="italic">house of Israel,</hi> and particularly those families in it that were cruel and oppressive. They unjustly devise evil against their brethren, and God will justly devise evil against them. Infinite Wisdom will so contrive the punishment of their sin that it shall be very sure, and such as cannot be avoided, very severe, and such as they cannot bear, very signal and remarkable, and such as shall be universally observed to answer to the sin. The more there appears of a wicked wit in the sin the more there shall appear of a holy wisdom and fitness in the punishment; for the Lord will be <hi type="italic">known by the judgments he executes;</hi> he will be owned by them. 1. He finds them very secure, and confident that they shall in some way or other escape the judgment, or, though they fall under it, shall soon throw it off and get clear of it, and therefore he tells them, It is <hi type="italic">an evil from which they shall not remove their neck.</hi> They were children of <hi type="italic">Belial,</hi> that would not endure the easy yoke of God's righteous commands, but <hi type="italic">broke those bonds</hi> asunder, and <hi type="italic">cast away those cords from them;</hi> and therefore God will lay upon them the heavy yoke of his righteous judgments, and they shall not be able to withdraw their necks from that; those that will not be overruled shall be overcome. 2. He finds them very proud and stately, and therefore he tells them that they shall not go haughtily, with <hi type="italic">stretched-forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa. iii. 16</reference>); for <hi type="italic">this time is evil,</hi> and the events of it are very humbling and mortifying, and such as will bring down the stoutest spirit. 3. He finds them very merry and jovial, and therefore tells them their note shall be changed, their laughter shall be turned into mourning and their joy into heaviness (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day,</hi> when God comes to punish you for your oppression, <hi type="italic">shall one take up a parable against you,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lament with a doleful lamentation,</hi> with <hi type="italic">a lamentation of lamentations</hi> (so the word is), a most lamentable lamentation, as a song of songs is a most pleasing song. Their enemies shall insult over them, and make a jest of their griefs, for they shall <hi type="italic">take up a parable against them.</hi> Their friends shall mourn over them, and lay to heart their calamities, and this shall be the general cry, "<hi type="italic">We are utterly spoiled;</hi> we are all undone." Note, Those that were most haughty and secure in their prosperity are commonly most dejected and most ready to despair in their adversity. 4. He finds them very rich in houses and lands, which they have gained by oppression, and therefore tells them that they shall be stripped of all. (1.) They shall, in their despair, give it all up; they shall say, <hi type="italic">We are utterly spoiled; he has changed the portion of my people,</hi> so that it is now no longer theirs, but it is in the possession and occupation of their enemies: <hi type="italic">How has he removed it from me!</hi> How suddenly, how powerfully! What is unjustly got by us will not long continue with us; the righteous God will remove it. <hi type="italic">Turning away</hi> from us in wrath, he <hi type="italic">has divided our fields,</hi> and given them into the hands of strangers. Woe to those from whom God turns away. The margin reads it, "<hi type="italic">Instead of restoring, he has divided our fields;</hi> instead of putting us again in the possession of our estates, he has confirmed those in the possession of them that have taken them from us." Note, It is just with God that those who have dealt fraudulently and violently with others should themselves be dealt fraudulently and violently with. (2.) God shall ratify what they say in their despair (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.5">v. 5</reference>); so it shall be: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt have none to cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the Lord,</hi> none to divide inheritances, because there shall be no inheritances to divide, no courts to try titles to lands, or determine controversies about them, or cast lots upon them, as in Joshua's time, for all shall be in the enemies' hand. This land, which should be taken from them, they had not only an unquestionable title to, but a very comfortable enjoyment of, for it was <hi type="italic">in the congregation of the Lord,</hi> or rather the congregation of the Lord was in it; it was God's land; it was a holy land, and therefore it was the more grievous to them to be turned out of it. Note, Those are to be considered the sorest calamities which cut us off from the congregation of the Lord, or cut us short in the enjoyment of the privileges of it.
entries.93eb008d450ece2e73621a00242f01def9e601c3: <div eID="gen20405" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Expostulation with the House of Jacob; The Sin and Punishment of Oppression. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  740.)</title> <div sID="gen20406" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Prophesy ye not, <hi type="italic">say they to them that</hi> prophesy: they shall not prophesy to them, <hi type="italic">that</hi> they shall not take shame. <hi type="super">7</hi> O <hi type="italic">thou that art</hi> named the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> straitened? <hi type="italic">are</hi> these his doings? do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly? <hi type="super">8</hi> Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war. <hi type="super">9</hi> The women of my people have ye cast out from their pleasant houses; from their children have ye taken away my glory for ever. <hi type="super">10</hi> Arise ye, and depart; for this <hi type="italic">is</hi> not <hi type="italic">your</hi> rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy <hi type="italic">you,</hi> even with a sore destruction. <hi type="super">11</hi> If a man walking in the spirit and falsehood do lie, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink; he shall even be the prophet of this people. <div eID="gen20406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20407" type="x-p"/> Here are two sins charged upon the people of Israel, and judgments denounced against them for each, such judgments as exactly answer the sin—persecuting God's prophets and oppressing God's poor. <div eID="gen20407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20408" type="x-p"/> I. Persecuting God's prophets, suppressing and silencing them, is a sin that provokes God as much as anything, for it not only spits in the face of his authority over us, but spurns at the bowels of his mercy to us; for his sending prophets to us is a sure and valuable token of his goodwill. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20409" type="x-p"/> 1. What the obstruction and opposition were which this people gave to God's prophets: They <hi type="italic">said to those that prophesy, Prophesy ye not,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa. xxx. 10</reference>. They <hi type="italic">said to the seers, "See not;</hi> do not trouble us with accounts of what you have seen, nor bring us any such frightful messages." They must either not prophesy at all or prophesy only what is pleasing. The word for <hi type="italic">prophesying</hi> here signifies <hi type="italic">dropping,</hi> for the words of the prophets dropped from heaven as the dew. Note, Those that hate to be reformed hate to be reproved, and do all they can to silence faithful ministers. Amos was forbidden to prophesy, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.10">Amos vii. 10</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> persecutors stop their breath, because they have no other way to stop their mouths; for, if they live, they will preach and torment those that dwell on the earth, as the <hi type="italic">two witnesses</hi> did, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>. Some read it, <hi type="italic">Prophesy not; let these prophesy.</hi> Let not those prophesy that tell us of our faults, and threaten us, but <hi type="italic">let those prophesy</hi> that will flatter us in our sins, and cry peace to us. They will not say that they will have no ministers at all, but they will have such as will say just what they would have them and go their way. This they are charged with (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">v. 11</reference>), that when they silenced and frowned upon the true prophets they countenanced and encouraged pretenders, and set them up, and made an interest for them, to confront God's faithful prophets: <hi type="italic">If a man walk in the spirit of falsehood,</hi> pretend to have the Spirit of God, while really it is a spirit of error, a spirit of delusion, and he himself knows that he has no commission, no instruction, from God, yet, if he says, <hi type="italic">I will prophesy unto thee of wine and strong drink,</hi> if he will but assure them that they shall have wine and strong drink enough, that they need not fear the judgments of war and famine which the other prophets threatened them with, that they shall always have plenty of the delights of sense and never know the want of them, and if he will but tell them that it is lawful for them to drink as much as they please of their wine and strong drink, and they need not scruple being drunk, that they <hi type="italic">shall have peace though they go on and add drunkenness to thirst,</hi> such a prophet as this is a man after their own heart, who will tell them that there is neither sin nor danger in the wicked course of life they lead: <hi type="italic">He shall even be the prophet of this people;</hi> such a man they would have to be their prophet, that will not only associate with them in their rioting and revellings, but will pretend to consecrate their sensualities by his prophecies and so harden them in their security and sensuality. Note, It is not strange if people that are vicious and debauched covet to have ministers that are altogether such as themselves, for they are willing to believe God is so too, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">Ps. l. 21</reference>. But how are sacred things profaned when they are prostituted to such base purposes, when prophecy itself shall be pressed into the services of a lewd and profane crew! But thus that servant who said, <hi type="italic">My Lord delays his coming,</hi> by the spirit of falsehood, <hi type="italic">smote his fellow servants</hi> and <hi type="italic">ate and drank with the drunken.</hi> <div eID="gen20409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20410" type="x-p"/> 2. How they are here expostulated with upon this matter (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O thou that art named the house of Jacob,</hi> does it become thee to say and do thus? Wilt thou silence those that prophesy, and forbid them to speak in God's name?" Note, It is an honour and privilege to be <hi type="italic">named of the house of Jacob.</hi> Thou art <hi type="italic">called a Jew,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.17">Rom. ii. 17</reference>. But, when those who are called by that worthy name degenerate, they commonly prove the worst of men themselves and the worst enemies to God's prophets. The Jews who were <hi type="italic">named of the house of Jacob</hi> were the most violent persecutors of the first preachers of the gospel. Upon this the prophet here argues with these oppressors of the word of God, and shows them, (1.) What an affront they hereby put upon God, the God of the holy prophets: "<hi type="italic">Is the Lord's Spirit straitened?</hi> In silencing the Lord's prophets you do what you can to silence his Spirit too; but do you think you can do it? Can you make the Spirit of God your prisoner and your servant? Will you prescribe to him what he shall say, and forbid him to say what is displeasing to you? If you silence the prophets, yet cannot the Spirit of the Lord find out other ways to reach your consciences? Can your unbelief frustrate the divine counsels?" (2.) What a scandal it was to their profession as Jews: "You are <hi type="italic">named the house of Jacob,</hi> and this is your honour; but <hi type="italic">are these his doings?</hi> Are these the doings of your father Jacob? Do you herein tread in his steps? No; if you were indeed his children you would do his works; but now you seek to kill and silence <hi type="italic">a man that tells you the truth,</hi> in God's name; <hi type="italic">this did not Abraham</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.39-John.8.40">John viii. 39, 40</reference>); this did not Jacob." Or, "<hi type="italic">Are these God's doings?</hi> Are these the doings that will please him? Are these the doings of his people? No, you know they are not, however some may be so strangely blinded and bigoted as to kill God's ministers and think that therein they <hi type="italic">do him service,</hi>" <reference osisRef="John.16.2">John xvi. 2</reference>. (3.) Let them consider how unreasonable and absurd the thing was in itself: <hi type="italic">Do not my words do good to those that walk uprightly?</hi> Yes; certainly they do; it is an appeal to the experiences of the <hi type="italic">generation of the upright: "Call now if there be any of them that will answer you, and to which of the saints will you turn?</hi> Turn to which you will, and you will find they all agree in this, that the word of God <hi type="italic">does good to those that walk uprightly;</hi> and will you then oppose that which does good, so much good as good preaching does? Herein you wrong God, who owns the words of the prophets to be his words (they are <hi type="italic">my words</hi>) and who by them aims and designs to do good to mankind (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.68">Ps. cxix. 68</reference>); and will you hinder the great benefactor from doing good? Will you put the light of the world under a bushel: You might as well say to the sun, Shine not, as <hi type="italic">say to the seers, See not.</hi> Herein you wrong the souls of men, and deprive them of the benefit designed them by the word of God." Note, Those are enemies not only to God, but to the world, they are enemies to their country, that silence good ministers, and obstruct the means of knowledge and grace; for it is certainly for the public common good of states and kingdoms that religion should be encouraged. God's words do good to those <hi type="italic">that walk uprightly.</hi> It is the character of good people that they <hi type="italic">walk uprightly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.15.2">Ps. xv. 2</reference>); and it is their comfort that the words of God are good and do good to them; they find comfort in them. God's words are good words to good people, and speak comfortably to them. But those that opposed the words of God, and silenced the prophets, pleaded, in justification of themselves, that God's words were unprofitable and unpleasant to them, and did them no good, nor prophesied any good concerning them, but evil, as Ahab complained of Micaiah, in answer to which the prophet here tells them that it was their own fault; they might thank themselves. They might find it of good use to them if they were but disposed to make a good use of it; if they would but walk uprightly, as they should, and so qualify themselves for comfort, the word of God would speak comfortably to them. <hi type="italic">Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise for the same.</hi> <div eID="gen20410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20411" type="x-p"/> 3. What they are threatened with for this sin; God also will choose their delusions, and, (1.) They shall be deprived of the benefit of a faithful ministry. Since they say, <hi type="italic">Prophesy not,</hi> God will take them at their word, and <hi type="italic">they shall not prophesy to them;</hi> their sin shall be their punishment. If men will silence God's ministers, it is just with God to silence them, as he did Ezekiel, and to say, They shall <hi type="italic">no more be reprovers</hi> and monitors to them. Let the physician no longer attend the patient that will not be healed, for he will not be ruled. They <hi type="italic">shall not prophesy to them,</hi> and then they will not take shame. As it is the work of magistrates, so it is also of ministers, to put men to shame when they do amiss (<reference osisRef="Judg.18.7">Judg. xviii. 7</reference>), that, being made ashamed of their folly, they may not return again to it; but, when God gives men up to be impudent and shameless in sin, he says to his prophets, <hi type="italic">They are joined to idols; let them alone.</hi> (2.) They shall be given up to the blind guidance of an unfaithful ministry. We may understand <reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">v. 11</reference> as a threatening: <hi type="italic">If a man be found walking in the spirit of falsehood,</hi> having such a lying spirit as was in the mouth of Ahab's prophets, that will strengthen their hands in their wicked ways, he <hi type="italic">shall be the prophet of this people,</hi> that is, God will leave them to themselves to hearken to such; since they will be deceived, let them be deceived; since they will not admit the <hi type="italic">truth in the love of it,</hi> God will send them <hi type="italic">strong delusions to believe a lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.11">2 Thess. ii. 10, 11</reference>. They shall have prophets that will prophesy to them for <hi type="italic">wine and strong drink</hi> (so some read it), that will give you a cast of their office to your mind for a bottle of wine of a flagon of ale, will soothe sinners in their sins if they will but feed them with the gratifications of their lusts; to have such prophets, and to be ridden by them, is as sad a judgment as any people can be under and as bad a preface of ruin approaching as it is to a particular person to be under the influence of a debauched conscience. <div eID="gen20411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20412" type="x-p"/> II. Oppressing God's poor is another sin they are charged with, as before (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.1-Mic.2.2">v. 1, 2</reference>), for it is a sin doubly hateful and provoking to God. Observe, <div eID="gen20412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20413" type="x-p"/> 1. How the sin is described, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.8-Mic.2.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. When they contemned God's prophets and opposed them they broke out into all other wickedness; what bonds will hold those that have no reverence for God's word? Those who formerly rose up against the enemies of the nation, in defence of their country and therein behaved themselves bravely, now of late <hi type="italic">rose up as enemies of the nation,</hi> and, instead of defending it, destroyed it, and did it more mischief (as usually such vipers in the bowels of a state do) than a foreign enemy could do. They made a prey of men, women, and children, (1.) Of men, that were travelling on the way, that <hi type="italic">pass by securely as men averse from war,</hi> that were far from any bad designs, but went peaceably about their lawful occasions; those they set upon, as if they had been dangerous obnoxious people, and <hi type="italic">pulled off the robe with the garment from them,</hi> that is, they stripped them both of the upper and the inner garment, took away <hi type="italic">their cloak,</hi> and would have <hi type="italic">their coat also;</hi> thus barbarously did they use those that were quiet in the land, who, being harmless, were fearless, and so the more easily make a prey of. (2.) Of women, whose sex should have been their protection (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The women of my people have you cast out from their pleasant houses. They devoured widows' houses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.14">Matt. xxiii. 14</reference>), and so turned them out of the possession of them, because they were pleasant houses, and such as they had a mind for. It was inhuman to deal thus barbarously with women; but that which especially aggravated it was that they were the women of <hi type="italic">God's people,</hi> whom they knew to be under his protection. (3.) Of children, whose age entitles them to a tender usage: <hi type="italic">From their children have you taken away my glory for ever.</hi> It was the glory of the Israelites' children that they were free, but they enslaved them—that they were born in God's house, and had a right to the privileges of it, but they sold them to strangers, sent them into idolatrous countries, where they were deprived for ever of that glory; at least the oppressors designed their captivity should be perpetual. Note, The righteous God will certainly reckon for injuries done to the widows and fatherless, who, being helpless and friendless, cannot otherwise expect to be righted. <div eID="gen20413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20414" type="x-p"/> 2. What the sentence is that is passed upon them for it (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Arise ye, and depart;</hi> prepare to quit this land, for you shall be forced out of it, as you have forced the women and children of my people out of their possessions; it is not, it shall not, be your rest, as it was intended that Canaan should be, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.11">Ps. xcv. 11</reference>. You shall have neither contentment nor continuance in it, <hi type="italic">because it is polluted</hi> by your wickedness." Sin is defiling to a land, and sinners cannot expect to rest in a land which they have polluted, but is will spew them out, as this land spewed out the Canaanites of old when they had polluted it with their abominations, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.27-Lev.18.28">Lev. xviii. 27, 28</reference>. "Nay, you shall not only be obliged to depart out of this land, but <hi type="italic">it shall destroy you even with a sore destruction;</hi> you shall either be turned out of it or (which is all one) you shall be ruined in it." We may apply this to our state in this present world; it is polluted; there is a great deal of <hi type="italic">corruption in the world, through lust,</hi> and therefore we should <hi type="italic">arise, and depart out of it,</hi> keep at a distance from the corruption that is in it, and <hi type="italic">keep ourselves unspotted</hi> from it. It <hi type="italic">is not our rest;</hi> it was never intended to be so; it was designed for our passage, but not for our portion—our inn, but not our home. Here <hi type="italic">we have no continuing city;</hi> let us therefore <hi type="italic">arise and depart;</hi> let us sit loose to it and live above it, and think of leaving it and seek a continuing city above.
entries.ab79ccf5470cc6a3ff08c5c419f3a544fa6ce318: <div eID="gen20414" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen20415" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of <hi type="italic">the multitude of</hi> men. <hi type="super">13</hi> The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> on the head of them. <div eID="gen20415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20416" type="x-p"/> After threatenings of wrath, the chapter here concludes, as is usual in the prophets, with promises of mercy, which were in part fulfilled when the Jews returned out of Babylon, and had their full accomplishment in the kingdom of the Messiah. Their grievances shall be all redressed. 1. Whereas they were dispersed, they shall be brought together again, and shall jointly receive the tokens of God's favour to them, and shall have communion with each other and comfort in each other (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will surely assemble, O Jacob! all of thee,</hi> all that belong to thee, all that are <hi type="italic">named of the house of Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">v. 7</reference>) that are now expelled your country, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">v. 10</reference>. I will bring you together again, and not one of you shall be lost, not one of you shall be missing. <hi type="italic">I will surely gather the remnant of Israel,</hi> that remnant that is designed and reserved for salvation; they shall be brought to incorporate in one body. <hi type="italic">I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah.</hi>" Sheep are inoffensive and sociable creatures; they shall be <hi type="italic">as the flock in the midst of their fold,</hi> where they are safe under the shepherd's eye and care; and <hi type="italic">they shall make great noise</hi> (as numerous flocks and herds do, with their bleating and lowing) <hi type="italic">by reason of the multitude of men</hi> (for the sheep are <hi type="italic">men,</hi> as the prophet explains this comparison, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.31">Ezek. xxxiv. 31</reference>), not by reason of their strifes and contentions, but by reason of their great numbers. This was accomplished when Christ by his gospel gathered together in one <hi type="italic">all the children of God that were scattered abroad,</hi> and united both Jews and Gentiles in one fold, and under one Shepherd, when all the complaint was that the <hi type="italic">place was too strait</hi> for them—that was <hi type="italic">the noise, by reason of their multitude</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.19-Isa.49.20">Isa. xlix. 19, 20</reference>), when there were some added to the church from all parts of the world, and all men were drawn to Christ by the attractive power of his cross, which shall be done yet more and more, and perfectly done, when he shall send forth his angels to <hi type="italic">gather in his elect from the four winds.</hi> 2. Whereas God had seemed to desert them, and cast them off, now he will own them, and head them, and help them through all the difficulties that are in the way of their return and deliverance (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">the breaker has come up before them,</hi> to break down all opposition, and clear the road for them; and under his guidance <hi type="italic">they have broken up, and have passed through the gate,</hi> the door of escape out of their captivity, and have <hi type="italic">gone out by it</hi> with courage and resolution, having Omnipotence for their van-guard. <hi type="italic">Their King shall pass before them,</hi> to head them in the way, even Jehovah (he was their king) <hi type="italic">on the head of them,</hi> as he was on the head of the armies of Israel when they followed the pillar of cloud and fire through the wilderness and when he appeared to Joshua as <hi type="italic">captain of the Lord's host.</hi> Christ is the church's King; he is Jehovah; he heads them, passes before them, brings them out of the land of their captivity, brings them into the land of their rest. He is the <hi type="italic">breaker,</hi> that broke through them, that rent the veil, and opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers. The learned bishop Pearson applies it to the resurrection of Christ, by which he obtained the power and became the pattern of our resurrection. <hi type="italic">The breaker has gone up before us</hi> out of the grave, and has carried away its gates, as Samson did Gaza's, bar and all, and by that breach we go out. The learned Dr. Pocock mentions, as the sense which some of the ancient Jews give of it, that the breaker is Elias, and their <hi type="italic">King</hi> the <hi type="italic">Messiah,</hi> the Son of David; and he thinks we may apply it to Christ and his forerunner <hi type="italic">John the Baptist.</hi> John was the breaker; he broke the ice, prepared the way of the Lord by the baptism of repentance; in him the gospel began; from his time <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven suffered violence;</hi> and so the Christian church is introduced, with <hi type="italic">Messiah the Prince</hi> before it, on the head of it, going forth <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer.</hi>  <chapter eID="Mic.2"/> <div eID="gen20416" type="x-p"/>

entries.3da510261d27401f05dac8b20368bf9640bbcbab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12731"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.2.1-Mic.2.13">Mi 2:1-13</reference>. Denunciation of the Evils Prevalent: The People's Unwillingness to Hear the Truth: Their Expulsion From the Land the Fitting Fruit of Their Sin: Yet Judah and Israel Are Hereafter to Be Restored.</title> <div sID="gen23571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12731"/><hi type="bold">1. devise ... work ... practise--</hi>They do evil not merely on a sudden impulse, but with deliberate design. As in the former chapter sins against the first table are reproved, so in this chapter sins against the second table. A gradation: "devise" is the conception of the evil purpose; "work" (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>), or "fabricate," the maturing of the scheme; "practise," or "effect," the execution of it.<div eID="gen23571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because it is in the power of their hand--</hi>for the phrase see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.29">Ge 31:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.27">Pr 3:27</reference>. Might, not right, is what regulates their conduct. Where they can, they commit oppression; where they do not, it is because they cannot. <div eID="gen23572" type="x-p"/>
entries.8335c3fde9a80bd272e79e7ed66b6005388d4bcb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12732"/><div sID="gen23573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12732"/>2. Parallelism, "Take by violence," answers to "take away"; "fields" and "houses," to "house" and "heritage" (that is, one's land). <div eID="gen23573" type="x-p"/>
entries.62237ba501c6c93f3d9ac78b5cee608533c2917f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12733"/><div sID="gen23574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12733"/><hi type="bold">3. against this family--</hi>against the nation, and especially against those reprobated in <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mi 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>.<div eID="gen23574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I devise an evil--</hi>a happy antithesis between God's dealings and the Jews' dealings (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mi 2:1</reference>). Ye "devise evil" against your fellow countrymen; I devise evil against you. Ye devise it wrongfully, I by righteous retribution in kind.<div eID="gen23575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from which ye shall not remove your necks--</hi>as ye have done from the law. The yoke I shall impose shall be one which ye cannot shake off. They who will not bend to God's "easy yoke" (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">30</reference>), shall feel His iron yoke.<div eID="gen23576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go haughtily--</hi>(Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.6.28">Jr 6:28</reference>). Ye shall not walk as now with neck haughtily uplifted, for the yoke shall press down your "neck."<div eID="gen23577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this time is evil--</hi>rather, "for that time shall be an evil time," namely, the time of the carrying away into captivity (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Am 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">Ep 5:16</reference>). <div eID="gen23578" type="x-p"/>
entries.156336e9281b604cc7a85766469a45fdf484c087: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12734"/><div sID="gen23579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12734"/><hi type="bold">4. one take up a parable against you--</hi>that is, Some of your foes shall do so, taking in derision from your own mouth your "lamentation," namely, "We be spoiled," &c.<div eID="gen23579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lament with a doleful lamentation--</hi>literally, "lament with a lamentation of lamentations." Hebrew, naha, nehi, nihyah, the repetition representing the continuous and monotonous wail.<div eID="gen23580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he hath changed the portion of my people--</hi>a charge of injustice against Jehovah. He transfers to other nations the sacred territory assigned as the rightful portion of our people (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.15">Mi 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turning away he hath divided our fields--</hi>Turning away from us to the enemy, He hath divided among them our fields. Calvin, as the Margin, explains, "Instead of restoring our territory, He hath divided our fields among our enemies, each of whom henceforward will have an interest in keeping what he hath gotten: so that we are utterly shut out from hope of restoration." Maurer translates as a noun, "He hath divided our fields to a rebel," that is, to the foe who is a rebel against the true God, and a worshipper of idols. So "backsliding," that is, backslider (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.4">Jr 49:4</reference>). English Version gives a good sense; and is quite tenable in the Hebrew. <div eID="gen23582" type="x-p"/>
entries.e744f8a331aa24fb8b09016ad6353577b3ca8dd6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12735"/><div sID="gen23583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12735"/><hi type="bold">5. Therefore--</hi>resumed from <reference osisRef="Mic.2.3">Mi 2:3</reference>. On account of your crimes described in <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mi 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>.<div eID="gen23583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou--</hi>the ideal individual ("me," <reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>), representing the guilty people in whose name he spoke.<div eID="gen23584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none that ... cast a cord by lot--</hi>none who shall have any possession measured out.<div eID="gen23585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the congregation of the Lord--</hi>among the people consecrated to Jehovah. By covetousness and violence (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">Mi 2:2</reference>) they had forfeited "the portion of Jehovah's people." This is God's implied answer to their complaint of injustice (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen23586" type="x-p"/>
entries.16746908cadefefaac75491a7374a41c184c5b9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12736"/><div sID="gen23587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12736"/><hi type="bold">6. Prophesy ye not, say they--</hi>namely, the Israelites say to the true prophets, when announcing unwelcome truths. Therefore God judicially abandons them to their own ways: "The prophets, by whose ministry they might have been saved from shame (ignominious captivity), shall not (that is, no longer) prophesy to them" (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Is 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.12">Am 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.16">7:16</reference>). Maurer translates the latter clause, "they shall not prophesy of such things" (as in <reference osisRef="Mic.2.3-Mic.2.5">Mi 2:3-5</reference>, these being rebellious Israel's words); "let them not prophesy"; "they never cease from insult" (from prophesying insults to us). English Version is supported by the parallelism: wherein the similarity of sound and word implies how exactly God makes their punishment answer to their sin, and takes them at their own word. "Prophesy," literally, "drop" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.2">Eze 21:2</reference>). <div eID="gen23587" type="x-p"/>
entries.30bd15bc834ad8145bbb313cc587d52c74be5c5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12737"/><div sID="gen23588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12737"/><hi type="bold">7. O thou ... named the house of Jacob--</hi>priding thyself on the name, though having naught of the spirit, of thy progenitor. Also, bearing the name which ought to remind thee of God's favors granted to thee because of His covenant with Jacob.<div eID="gen23588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is the Spirit of the Lord straitened?--</hi>Is His compassion contracted within narrower limits now than formerly, so that He should delight in your destruction (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.77.7-Ps.77.9">Psa 77:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.1">Is 59:1</reference>, 2)?<div eID="gen23589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are these his doings?--</hi>that is, Are such threatenings His delight? Ye dislike the prophets' threatenings (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.6">Mi 2:6</reference>): but who is to blame? Not God, for He delights in blessing, rather than threatening; but yourselves (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.8">Mi 2:8</reference>) who provoke His threatenings [Grotius]. Calvin translates, "Are your doings such as are prescribed by Him?" Ye boast of being God's peculiar people: Do ye then conform your lives to God's law?<div eID="gen23590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly--</hi>Are not My words good to the upright? If your ways were upright, My words would not be threatening (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Psa 18:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.19">Mt 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>). <div eID="gen23591" type="x-p"/>
entries.52a2984f486cba682ea6eb37eb811c82140a7ce8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12738"/><div sID="gen23592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12738"/>8. Your ways are not such that I can deal with you as I would with the upright.<div eID="gen23592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23593" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Even of late--</hi>literally, "yesterday," "long ago." So "of old." Hebrew, "yesterday" (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>); "heretofore," Hebrew, "since yesterday" (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.4">Jos 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen23593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my people is risen up as an enemy--</hi>that is, has rebelled against My precepts; also has become an enemy to the unoffending passers-by.<div eID="gen23594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">robe with the garment--</hi>Not content with the outer "garment," ye greedily rob passers-by of the ornamental "robe" fitting the body closely and flowing down to the feet [Ludovicus De Dieu] (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.40">Mt 5:40</reference>).<div eID="gen23595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as men averse from war--</hi>in antithesis to (My people) "as an enemy." Israel treats the innocent passers-by, though "averse from war," as an enemy" would treat captives in his power, stripping them of their habiliments as lawful spoils. Grotius translates, "as men returning from war," that is, as captives over whom the right of war gives the victors an absolute power. English Version is supported by the antithesis. <div eID="gen23596" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb53cfdd01264d8df2d4c7a5919a614edac9a048: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12739"/><div sID="gen23597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12739"/><hi type="bold">9. The women of my people--</hi>that is, the widows of the men slain by you (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">Mi 2:2</reference>) ye cast out from their homes which had been their delight, and seize on them for yourselves.<div eID="gen23597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from their children--</hi>that is, from the orphans of the widows.<div eID="gen23598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken away my glory--</hi>namely, their substance and raiment, which, being the fruit of God's blessing on the young, reflected God's glory. Thus Israel's crime was not merely robbery, but sacrilege. Their sex did not save the women, nor their age the children from violence.<div eID="gen23599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>There was no repentance. They persevered in sin. The pledged garment was to be restored to the poor before sunset (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.26">Ex 22:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.27">27</reference>); but these never restored their unlawful booty. <div eID="gen23600" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb1202d80e4aabcfd406d735c3ea378807bee8ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12740"/><div sID="gen23601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12740"/><hi type="bold">10. Arise ye, and depart--</hi>not an exhortation to the children of God to depart out of an ungodly world, as it is often applied; though that sentiment is a scriptural one. This world is doubtless not our "rest," being "polluted" with sin: it is our passage, not our portion; our aim, not our home (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">2Co 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">He 13:14</reference>). The imperatives express the certainty of the future event predicted. "Since such are your doings (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>, &c.), My sentence on you is irrevocable (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>), however distasteful to you (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.6">Mi 2:6</reference>); ye who have cast out others from their homes and possessions (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">Mi 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">8, 9</reference>) must arise, depart, and be cast out of your own (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>): for this is not your rest" (<reference osisRef="Num.10.33">Nu 10:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.9">De 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.95.11">Psa 95:11</reference>). Canaan was designed to be a rest to them after their wilderness fatigues. But it is to be so no longer. Thus God refutes the people's self-confidence, as if God were bound to them inseparably. The promise (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Psa 132:14</reference>) is quite consistent with temporary withdrawal of God from Israel for their sins.<div eID="gen23601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall destroy you--</hi>The land shall spew you out, because of the defilements wherewith ye "polluted" it (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">Le 18:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">Jr 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.12-Ezek.36.14">Eze 36:12-14</reference>). <div eID="gen23602" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c75788caeb0977235595aeca4a04b64b38e79bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12741"/><div sID="gen23603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12741"/><hi type="bold">11. walking in the spirit--</hi>The Hebrew means also "wind." "If a man professing to have the 'spirit' of inspiration (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.3">Eze 13:3</reference>; so 'man of the spirit,' that is, one claiming inspiration, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Ho 9:7</reference>), but really walking in 'wind' (prophecy void of nutriment for the soul, and unsubstantial as the wind) and falsehood, do lie, saying (that which ye like to hear), I will prophesy," &c., even such a one, however false his prophecies, since he flatters your wishes, shall be your prophet (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.2.6">Mi 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jr 5:31</reference>).<div eID="gen23603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophesy ... of wine--</hi>that is, of an abundant supply of wine. <div eID="gen23604" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8057e71bd1a8a0f71bf52272044d54f874f5b04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12742"/><div sID="gen23605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12742"/>12. A sudden transition from threats to the promise of a glorious restoration. Compare a similar transition in <reference osisRef="Hos.1.9">Ho 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>. Jehovah, too, prophesies of good things to come, but not like the false prophets, "of wine and strong drink" (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">Mi 2:11</reference>). After I have sent you into captivity as I have just threatened, I will thence assemble you again (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6">Mi 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen23605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all of thee--</hi>The restoration from Babylon was partial. Therefore that here meant must be still future, when "all Israel shall be saved" (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>). The restoration from "Babylon" (specified (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.10">Mi 4:10</reference>) is the type of the future one.<div eID="gen23606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jacob ... Israel--</hi>the ten tribes' kingdom (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">Ho 12:2</reference>) and Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.19.8">2Ch 19:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.2">21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen23607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remnant--</hi>the elect remnant, which shall survive the previous calamities of Judah, and from which the nation is to spring into new life (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Is 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20-Isa.10.22">10:20-22</reference>).<div eID="gen23608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the sheep of Bozrah--</hi>a region famed for its rich pastures (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4">2Ki 3:4</reference>). Gesenius for Bozrah translates, "sheepfold." But thus there will be tautology unless the next clause be translated, "in the midst of their pasture." English Version is more favored by the Hebrew. <div eID="gen23609" type="x-p"/>
entries.01789f6d2174cf9084508c884eccde2c5e30dae4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12743"/><div sID="gen23610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12743"/><hi type="bold">13. The breaker--</hi>Jehovah-Messiah, who breaks through every obstacle in the way of their restoration: not as formerly breaking forth to destroy them for transgression (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.22">Ex 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.21.15">Jud 21:15</reference>), but breaking a way for them through their enemies.<div eID="gen23610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>the returning Israelites and Jews.<div eID="gen23611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passed through the gate--</hi>that is, through the gate of the foe's city in which they had been captives. So the image of the resurrection (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">Ho 13:14</reference>) represents Israel's restoration.<div eID="gen23612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their king--</hi>"the Breaker," peculiarly "their king" (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.37">Mt 27:37</reference>).<div eID="gen23613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pass before them--</hi>as He did when they went up out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Ex 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">De 1:30</reference>, 33).<div eID="gen23614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23615" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord on the head of them--</hi>Jehovah at their head (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Is 52:12</reference>). Messiah, the second person, is meant (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.23.20">Ex 23:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.14">33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>). <chapter eID="Mic.2"/>

entries.4e3992f1b8c13bd6176deaab015935344cf3efb6: <div eID="gen34733" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34734" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34735" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34735" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34734" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34736" type="x-p"/> Here the prophet denounces a wo against the plotters of wickedness, the covetous and the oppressor, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mic 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">Mic 2:2</reference>. God is represented as devising their ruin, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.3">Mic 2:3</reference>. An Israelite is then introduced as a mourner, personating his people, and lamenting their fate, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mic 2:4</reference>. Their total expulsion is now threatened on account of their very numerous offenses, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.5-Mic.2.10">Mic 2:5-10</reference>. Great infatuation of the people in favor of those pretenders to Divine inspiration who prophesied to them peace and plenty, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">Mic 2:11</reference>. The chapter concludes with a gracious promise of the restoration of the posterity of Jacob from captivity; possibly alluding to their deliverance from the Chaldean yoke, an event which was about two hundred years in futurity at the delivery of this prophecy, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">Mic 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mic 2:13</reference>. <div eID="gen34736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34738" type="x-p"/> Wo to them that devise iniquity - Who lay schemes and plans for transgressions; who make it their study to find out new modes of sinning; and make these things their nocturnal meditations, that, having fixed their plan, they may begin to execute it as soon as it is light in the morning. <div eID="gen34738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34739" type="x-p"/> Because it is in the power of their hand - They think they may do whatever they have power and opportunity to do.
entries.86de5d1da0f40a230c185ffbeccddb732214ca68: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34740" type="x-p"/> They covet fields - These are the rich and mighty in the land; and, like Ahab, they will take the vineyard or inheritance of any poor Naboth on which they may fix their covetous eye; so that they take away even the heritage of the poor.
entries.2fdf452019a00bd66ed2fd83a06d6724ffaf113e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34741" type="x-p"/> Against this family (the Israelites) do I devise an evil - You have devised the evil of plundering the upright; I will devise the evil to you of punishment for your conduct; you shall have your necks brought under the yoke of servitude. Tiglath-pileser ruined this kingdom, and transported the people to Assyria, under the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah; and Micah lived to see this catastrophe. See on <reference osisRef="Mic.2.9">Mic 2:9</reference> (note).
entries.7064b97ec5e850082d0c2b6435d92cd3a616999f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34742" type="x-p"/> Take up a parable against you - Your wickedness and your punishment shall be subjects of common conversation; and a funeral dirge shall be composed and sung for you as for the dead. The lamentation is that which immediately follows: We be utterly spoiled; and ends, Are these his doings? <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mic 2:7</reference>.
entries.419d217c4d35dddc31df43d0e710cca2e3cd0ed8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34743" type="x-p"/> None that shall cast a cord - You will no more have your inheritance divided to you by lot, as it was to your fathers; ye shall neither have fields nor possessions of any kind.
entries.0a7539dbb5b81f352c94eea448d377ac4e58e458: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34744" type="x-p"/> Prophesy ye not - Do not predict any more evils - we have as many as we can bear. We are utterly ruined - shame and confusion cover our faces. The original is singular, and expressive of sorrow and sobbing. Literally, "Do not cause it to rain; they will cause it to rain; they cannot make it rain sooner than this; confusion shall not depart from us." To rain, often means to preach, to prephesy; <reference osisRef="Eze.20.46">Eze 20:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.21.2">Eze 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amo.7.16">Amo 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.32.2">Deu 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.22">Job 29:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.5.3">Pro 5:3</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen34744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34745" type="x-p"/> The last line Bp. Newcome translates, "For he shall not remove from himself reproaches;" and paraphrases, "The true prophet will subject himself to public disgrace by exercising his office."
entries.a34e5829e3f632898daa3798fa79f4a817b7b5a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34746" type="x-p"/> Is the Spirit of the Lord straitened? - This is the complaint of the Israelites, and a part of the lamentation. Doth it not speak by other persons as well as by Micah? Doth it communicate to us such influences as it did formerly? Is it true that these evils are threatened by that Spirit? Are these his doings? To which Jehovah answers, "Do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly?" No upright man need fear any word spoken by me: my words to such yield instruction and comfort; never dismay. Were ye upright, ye would not complain of the words of my prophets. The last clause may be translated, "Walking with him that is upright." The upright man walks by the word; and the word walks with him who walks by it.
entries.76d3b9737d688a5c817d28c39a93ca8846944f68: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34747" type="x-p"/> My people is risen up as an enemy - Ye are not only opposed to me, but ye are enemies to each other. Ye rob and spoil each other. Ye plunder the peaceable passenger; depriving him both of his upper and under garment; ye pull off the robe from those who, far from being spoilers themselves, are averse from war.
entries.cbc988b7ce29ec48477195da0306141ebf0d0604: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34748" type="x-p"/> The women of my people - Ye are the cause of the women and their children being carried into captivity - separated from their pleasant habitations, and from my temple and ordinances - and from the blessings of the covenant, which it is my glory to give, and theirs to receive. These two verses may probably relate to the war made on Ahaz by Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel. They fell suddenly upon the Jews; killed in one day one hundred and twenty thousand, and took two hundred thousand captive; and carried away much spoil. Thus, they rose up against them as enemies, when there was peace between the two kingdoms; spoiled them of their goods, carried away men, women, and children, till, at the remonstrances of the prophet Oded, they were released. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.6">2Chr 28:6</reference>, etc. Micah lived in the days of Ahaz, and might have seen the barbarities which he here describes.
entries.bf9ba522f70b089dfd919b2cef67bc1c933b9501: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34749" type="x-p"/> Arise ye, and depart - Prepare for your captivity; ye shall have no resting place here: the very land is polluted by your iniquities, and shall vomit you out, and it shall be destroyed; and the destruction of it shall be great and sore. <div eID="gen34749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34750" type="x-p"/> Some think this is an exhortation to the godly, to leave a land that was to be destroyed so speedily.
entries.6d12ac719686efc73b04e072e2e7d543e0989828: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34751" type="x-p"/> If a man walking in the spirit and falsehood - The meaning is: If a man who professes to be Divinely inspired do lie, by prophesying of plenty, etc., then such a person shall be received as a true prophet by this people. It not unfrequently happens that the Christless worldling, who has got into the priest's office for a maintenance, and who leaves the people undisturbed in their unregenerate state, is better received than the faithful pastor, who proclaims the justice of the Lord, and the necessity of repentance and forsaking sin, in order to their being made partakers of that holiness without which no man shall see God.
entries.72612c7cbd07f2adac07aafe7bf9f186f63a4bfe: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34752" type="x-p"/> I will surely assemble - This is a promise of the restoration of Israel from captivity. He compares them to a flock of sheep rushing together to their fold, the hoofs of which make a wonderful noise or clatter. So when one hundred sheep run, eight hundred toes or divisions of these bifid animals make a clattering noise. This appears to be the image.
entries.c245eef709f51f74b9306cd476e49e826f30e467: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34753" type="x-p"/> The breaker is come up - He who is to give them deliverance, and lead them out on the way of their return. He who takes down the hurdles, or makes a gap in the wall or hedge, to permit them to pass through. This may apply to those human agents that shall permit and order their return. And Jehovah being at their head, may refer to their final restoration, when the Lord Jesus shall become their leader, they having returned unto him as the shepherd and bishop of their souls; and they and the Gentiles forming one fold under one shepherd, to go no more out into captivity for ever. Lord, hasten the time!  <chapter eID="Mic.2"/> <div eID="gen34753" type="x-p"/>

entries.4a45ae5e24d08bb8d11abfb809779fd5b07a90f6: Mic 2:1-2 <div eID="gen16541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16542" type="x-p"/> The violent acts of the great men would be punished by God with the withdrawal of the inheritance of His people, or the loss of Canaan. Mic 2:1. <hi type="italic">“Woe to those who devise mischief, and prepare evil upon their beds! In the light of the morning they carry it out, for their hand is their God.</hi> Mic 2:2. <hi type="italic">They covet fields and plunder; them, and houses and take them; and oppress the man and his house, the man and his inheritance.” </hi> The woe applies to the great and mighty of the nation, who by acts of injustice deprive the common people of the inheritance conferred upon them by the Lord (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa 5:8</reference>). The prophet describes them as those who devise plans by night upon their beds for robbing the poor, and carry them out as soon as the day dawns. חשׁב און denotes the sketching out of plans (see <reference osisRef="Ps.36.5">Psa 36:5</reference>); and פּעל רע, to work evil, the preparation of the ways and means for carrying out their wicked plans. פּעל, the preparation, is distinguished from עשׁה, the execution, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Isa 41:4</reference>, for which יצר and עשׂה are also used (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.43.7">Isa 43:7</reference>). “Upon their beds,” i.e., by night, the time of quiet reflection (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.5">Psa 4:5</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.4.13">Job 4:13</reference>). “By the light of the morning,” i.e., at daybreak, without delay. כּי ישׁ וגו, lit., “for their hand is for a god,” i.e., their power passes as a god to them; they know of no higher power than their own arm; whatever they wish it is in their power to do (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.31.29">Gen 31:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.27">Pro 3:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Hab 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>). Ewald and Rückert weaken the thought by adopting the rendering, “because it stands free in their hand;” and Hitzig’s rendering, “if it stands in their hand,” is decidedly false. <hi type="italic">Kı̄</hi> cannot be a conditional particle here, because the thought would thereby be weakened in a manner quite irreconcilable with the context. In Mic 2:2 the evil which they plan by night, and carry out by day, is still more precisely defined. By force and injustice they seize upon the property (fields, houses) of the poor, the possessions which the Lord has given to His people for their inheritance. <hi type="italic">Châmad</hi> points to the command against coveting (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.14-Exod.20.17">Exo 20:14-17</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.5.18">Deu 5:18</reference>). The second half of the verse (Mic 2:2) contains a conclusion drawn from the first: “and so they practise violence upon the man and his property.” <hi type="italic">Bēth</hi> answers to <hi type="italic">bottı̄m</hi>, and <hi type="italic">nachălâh</hi> to the <hi type="italic">Sâdōth</hi>, as their hereditary portion in the land - the portion of land which each family received when Canaan was divided.
entries.e369a5cdcbea4b5d5204d05b34918ca2a792eb92: Mic 2:3-4 <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith Jehovah, Behold, I devise evil concerning this family, from which ye shall not withdraw your necks, and not walk loftily, for it is an evil time. </hi> Mic 2:4. <hi type="italic">In that day will men raise against you a proverb, and lament a lamentation. It has come to pass, they say; we are waste, laid waste; the inheritance of my people he exchanges: how does he withdraw it from me! To the rebellious one he divides our field.”</hi> The punishment introduced with <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) will correspond to the sin. Because they reflect upon evil, to deprive their fellow-men of their possessions, Jehovah will bring evil upon this generation, lay a heavy yoke upon their neck, out of which they will not be able to necks, and under which they will not be able to walk loftily, or with extended neck. המּשׁפּחה הזּאת is not this godless family, but the whole of the existing nation, whose corrupt members are to be exterminated by the judgment (see Isa 29:20.). The yoke which the Lord will bring upon them is subjugation to the hostile conqueror of the land and the oppression of exile (see <reference osisRef="Jer.27.12">Jer 27:12</reference>). <hi type="italic">Hâlakh rōmâh</hi>, to walk on high, i.e., with the head lifted up, which is a sign of pride and haughtiness. <hi type="italic">Rōmâh</hi> is different from קוממיּוּת, an upright attitude, in Lev 27:13. כּי עת רעה, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amo 5:13</reference>, but in a different sense, is not used of moral depravity, but of the distress which will come upon Israel through the laying on of the yoke. Then will the opponents raise derisive songs concerning Israel, and Israel itself will bewail its misery. The verbs <hi type="italic">yissâ'</hi>, <hi type="italic">nâhâh</hi>, and <hi type="italic">'âmar</hi> are used impersonally. <hi type="italic">Mâshâl</hi> is not synonymous with <hi type="italic">nehı̄</hi>, a mournful song (Ros.), but signifies a figurative saying, a proverb-song, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Isa 14:4</reference>; Hab 2:6. The subject to ישּׂא is the opponents of Israel, hence עליכם; on the other hand, the subject to <hi type="italic">nâhâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">'âmar</hi> is the Israelites themselves, as נשׁדּנוּ teaches. נהיה is not a feminine formation from נהי, a mournful song, <hi type="italic">lamentum lamenti</hi>, i.e., a mournfully mournful song, as Rosenmüller, Umbreit, and the earlier commentators suppose; but the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> of היה (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.8.27">Dan 8:27</reference>): <hi type="italic">actum est!</hi> it is all over! - an exclamation of despair (Le de Dieu, Ewald, etc.); and it is written after <hi type="italic">'âmar</hi>, because נהיה as an exclamation is equivalent in meaning to an object. The omission of the copula <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> precludes our taking <hi type="italic">'âmar</hi> in connection with what follows (Maurer). The following clauses are a still further explanation of נהיה: we are quite laid waste. The form נשׁדּנוּ for נשׁדּונוּ is probably chosen simply to imitate the tone of lamentation better (Hitzig). The inheritance of my people, i.e., the land of Canaan, He (Jehovah) changes, i.e., causes it to pass over to another possessor, namely, to the heathen. The words receive their explanation from the clauses which follow: How does He cause (sc., the inheritance) to depart from me! Not how does He cause me to depart. לשׁובב is not an infinitive, <hi type="italic">ad reddendum</hi>, or <hi type="italic">restituendum</hi>, which is altogether unsuitable, but <hi type="italic">nomen verbale</hi>, the fallen or rebellious one, like שׁובבה in <reference osisRef="Jer.31.22">Jer 31:22</reference>; Jer 49:4. This is the term applied by mourning Israel to the heathenish foe, to whom Jehovah apportions the fields of His people. The withdrawal of the land is the just punishment for the way in which the wicked great men have robbed the people of their inheritance.
entries.a768afde3a3b87ffa4a08f19b7eff9423f840f99: Mic 2:5 <hi type="italic">“Therefore wilt thou have none to cast a measure for the lot in the congregation of Jehovah.” </hi> With <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) the threat, commenced with <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> in Mic 2:3, is resumed and applied to individual sinners. The whole nation is not addressed in לך, still less the prophet, as Hitzig supposes, but every individual among the tyrannical great men (Mic 2:1, Mic 2:2). The singular is used instead of the plural, to make the address more impressive, that no one may imagine that he is excepted from the threatened judgment. For a similar transition from the plural to the singular, see Mic 3:10. The expression, to cast the measure <hi type="italic">begōrâl</hi>, i.e., in the nature of a lot (equivalent to for a lot, or as a lot), may be explained on the ground that the land was divided to the Israelites by lot, and then the portion that fell to each tribe was divided among the different families by measure. The words are not to be taken, however, as referring purely to the future, as Caspari supposes, i.e., to the time when the promised land would be divided afresh among the people on their return. For even if the prophet does proclaim in Mic 2:12, Mic 2:13 the reassembling of Israel and its restoration to its hereditary land, this thought cannot be arbitrarily taken for granted here. We therefore regard the words as containing a general threat, that the ungodly will henceforth receive no further part in the inheritance of the Lord, but that they are to be separated from the congregation of Jehovah.
entries.86682de2ac369d2f1212a2b60d3a11f7b2a47745: Mic 2:6-7 <div eID="gen16542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16543" type="x-p"/> As such a prophecy as this met with violent contradiction, not only from the corrupt great men, but also from the false prophets who flattered the people, Micah indicates it by showing that the people are abusing the long-suffering and mercy of the Lord; and that, by robbing the peaceable poor, the widows, and the orphans, they are bringing about the punishment of banishment out of the land. Mic 2:6. <hi type="italic">“Drip not (prophesy not), they drip: if they drip not this, the shame will not depart.</hi> Mic 2:7. <hi type="italic">Thou, called house of Jacob, is the patience of Jehovah short, then? or is this His doing? Are not my words good to him that walketh uprightly?” </hi>הטּיף, to drip, to cause words to flow, used of prophesying, as in Amo 7:16. The speakers in <hi type="italic">Mic 2:6</hi> are not the Jews generally, or the rich oppressors who have just been punished and threatened. The word <hi type="italic">yattı̄phū</hi> does not agree with this, since it does not mean to chatter, but to prophesy, as Mic 2:11 and also the primary passage <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">Deu 32:2</reference> show. But Micah could not call the rich men’s speaking prophesying. It is rather false prophets who are speaking, - namely, those who in the word <hi type="italic">'al</hi>-<hi type="italic">tattı̄phū</hi> (prophesy not) would prohibit the true prophets from predicting the judgments of the Lord. The second hemistich is rendered by most of the modern commentators, “they are not to chatter (preach) of such things; the reproaches cease not,” or “there is no end to reproaching” (Ewald, Hitzig, Maurer, and Caspari). But this is open to the following objections: (1) That הטּיף ל in Mic 2:11 means to prophesy to a person (not concerning or of anything); (2) that <hi type="italic">sūg</hi> or <hi type="italic">nâsag</hi> means to depart, not to cease; (3) that even the thought, “the reproaches to not cease,” is apparently unsuitable, since Micah could not well call a prohibition against prophesying an incessant reproach; and to this we may add, (4) the grammatical harshness of taking לא יטּיפוּ as an imperative, and the following לא יסּג as an indicative (a simple declaration). Still less can the rendering, “they (the true prophets) will not chatter about this, yet the reproach will not depart” (Ros., Rückert), be vindicated, as such an antithesis as this would necessarily be indicated by a particle. The only course that remains, therefore, is that adopted by C. B. Michaelis and Hengstenberg, viz., to take the words as conditional: if they (the true prophets) do not prophesy to these (the unrighteous rich in Mic 2:1, Mic 2:2 : Hengstenberg), or on account of these things (Michaelis), the shame will not depart, i.e., shameful destruction will burst incessantly upon them. On the absence of the conditional אם, see Ewald, p. 357, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. Such addresses as these do not please the corrupt great men; but they imagine that such threats are irreconcilable with the goodness of Jehovah. This is the connection of Mic 2:7, in which the prophet meets the reproach cast upon his threatening words with the remark, that God is not wrathful, and has no love for punishing, but that He is stirred up to wrath by the sins of the nation, and obliged to punish. האמוּר is not an exclamation, “O, what is said! = O for such talk as this!” (Ewald, Umbreit, Caspari); for it cannot be shown that the participle is ever used in this way, and it cannot be supported from הפכּכם in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">Isa 29:16</reference>, especially as here a second vocative would follow. Nor is it a question: <hi type="italic">Num dicendum?</hi> Dare one say this?” (Hitzig).
